items.title: Hardy bacterium survives Mars-like asteroid blast in lab

featured_image.name: Asteroid Impacts Could Launch Living Microbes From Mars

items.description:
A resilient desert bacterium survived pressures equivalent to being blasted off the surface of Mars by an asteroid strike, according to a new study from Johns Hopkins University, lending fresh support to the idea that life could travel between planets aboard space debris.

The research, published Monday in PNAS Nexus, found that the extremophile Deinococcus radiodurans — a bacterium found in the high deserts of Chile — achieved nearly 100% survival at 1.4 Gigapascals of pressure and 60% survival at 2.4 Gigapascals, far exceeding what scientists had thought possible. By comparison, other commonly studied microorganisms such as E. coli and Shewanella oneidensis showed survival rates below 10% at similar pressures.[1][2]

items.title: Russia's Medvedev warns of World War III over US strikes on Iran

featured_image.name: Trump slams Russia's Medvedev for claiming countries will give Iran nuclear warheads

items.description: As U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran entered their fourth day, Russia's Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned that World War III "will undoubtedly begin" if President Donald Trump "continues his insane course of criminally changing political regimes," while analysts said the widening conflict is undermining Washington's ability to deter China in the Pacific.

items.title: Israel sends ground forces into southern Lebanon amid Hezbollah clashes

featured_image.name: Labanon-Israel.jpg

items.description:
Israeli troops crossed into southern Lebanon on Tuesday, seizing new positions beyond the border as the military expanded its campaign against Hezbollah following days of rocket and drone attacks that have opened a second front in the broader U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

The Israel Defense Forces said soldiers from the 91st "Galilee" Division entered southern Lebanon and captured several strategic points as part of what the military called an "enhanced forward defense posture," moving beyond five outposts Israel has maintained since a ceasefire was reached in November 2024. Eyewitnesses told Xinhua that an Israeli force including a tank and three military bulldozers crossed the Blue Line at around 8:00 a.m. local time, advancing roughly one kilometer into Lebanese territory near the town of Tal al-Nahas.[1][2][3]

items.title: US closes embassies in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia amid Iranian drone strikes

featured_image.name: US Embassy in Riyadh, Omani port hit by drones; US base in Bahrain targeted

items.description:
The U.S. Embassy in Kuwait was struck by at least one drone on Monday, sparking a large fire at the compound and prompting the mission to close indefinitely as Iran's retaliatory attacks against American interests in the Gulf entered a third consecutive day.

Three diplomatic sources confirmed to AFP that the embassy compound in Kuwait City was hit by drones on March 2, with smoke seen billowing from the area. No injuries were reported, according to a U.S. official, and staff had been ordered to return to their residences and shelter in place before the fire broke out, leaving few if any employees inside the main building at the time.[1][2][3]

items.title: Researchers use 270-year-old physics trick to build longer-lasting sodium batteries

featured_image.name: 270-year-old physics trick leads to affordable sodium ...

items.description: An international team of scientists has harnessed a centuries-old physics phenomenon to build a sodium-ion battery cathode that lasts over 10,000 charge-discharge cycles, a development that could help wean large-scale energy storage off scarce lithium. The study, published in the journal Small, brings together researchers from India's IISER Bhopal and IIT Gandhinagar, Swansea University in the UK, and the University of Southern Queensland in Australia.[1]

items.title: Bank of Japan may delay rate hike as Iran war roils markets

featured_image.name: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures sink as Iran conflict escalates

items.description:
The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran has sent shockwaves through global energy and financial markets, with crude oil prices surging and investors scrambling for safe-haven assets as the conflict enters its fourth day with no sign of de-escalation.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, spiked as much as 13% over the weekend before settling with gains of roughly 9% on Monday, climbing into the upper $70s per barrel. The surge came as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint through which roughly 20% of the world's daily oil supply passes. Tanker traffic through the strait dropped to near zero, with more than 150 ships anchoring outside to avoid the risks.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Oil tops $82 as Iran conflict threatens Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: Oil prices rise sharply after US, Israeli attacks on Iran

items.description:
Oil prices surged to their highest levels since early 2025 this week as an expanding military conflict between the United States and Israel on one side and Iran on the other rattled global energy markets and raised fears of prolonged supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude closed Monday's session up roughly 6.7%, after earlier spiking as much as 13% to above $82 per barrel — its highest point since January 2025, according to Reuters. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude also climbed more than 6% on Monday. By Tuesday, prices continued to rise, with Brent topping $82 a barrel as concerns mounted over the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.[1][2]

items.title: IAEA confirms damage at Iran's Natanz nuclear site

featured_image.name: Iran's Natanz nuclear site hit: Tehran vows to rebuild ...

items.description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed on Tuesday that entrance buildings at Iran's underground Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant sustained damage during the ongoing U.S.-Israeli military campaign, but said no radiological consequences are expected.

"Based on the latest available satellite imagery, IAEA can now confirm some recent damage to entrance buildings of Iran's underground Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant (FEP)," the agency wrote on X. "No radiological consequence expected and no additional impact detected at FEP itself, which was severely damaged in the June conflict."[1]

items.title: Asian shares fall as Iran war chokes global oil supply

featured_image.name: Oil prices surge, but no panic yet, as Iran war continues - NPR

items.description:
The U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, now entering its fourth day, has sent shockwaves through global energy and financial markets, with oil prices surging, the Strait of Hormuz effectively shut to commercial shipping, and investors scrambling for safe-haven assets.

Brent crude spiked as much as 13% over the weekend before settling around $79 per barrel on Monday, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude jumped roughly 8%. Analysts at Barclays and Rystad Energy have warned that prices could reach $100 a barrel if disruptions persist. On Tuesday in Asia, oil prices continued climbing, with Brent adding another $1.10 to near $79.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: India cuts industrial gas supply after Qatar halts LNG production

featured_image.name: Qatar suspended liquefied natural gas (LNG) production on ...

items.description:
Indian energy companies on Tuesday slashed natural gas deliveries to industrial consumers by 10 to 30 percent after Qatar — the country's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas — halted all LNG production following Iranian drone strikes on two major facilities.[1][2]

Petronet LNG, India's top LNG importer, notified GAIL, the leading gas marketing firm, and other companies of reduced supplies late Monday, according to Reuters, citing four industry sources. GAIL and Indian Oil Corporation then relayed the cuts to their downstream customers.[2][3][1]

items.title: China set to lower growth target as parliament opens

featured_image.name: China's leaders vow support for economy, crackdown on ...

items.description: China is poised to trim its economic growth target for the first time in four years when Premier Li Qiang delivers the government work report at the opening of the National People's Congress on March 5. Most analysts expect Beijing to set a 2026 GDP growth target of 4.5% to 5%, a step down from the "around 5%" goal maintained over the past three years.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Israel's Iron Beam laser utilised in combat for first time

featured_image.name: Israel plans to deploy Iron Beam laser defence system by ...

items.description: Israel's Iron Beam laser defense system saw its first operational use in combat early Monday as it helped intercept aerial threats launched by Hezbollah from Lebanon, marking a milestone for directed-energy weapons in warfare. The deployment came as the Middle East plunged deeper into crisis following the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in a joint U.S.-Israeli strike on February 28.

items.title: UT Austin physicists confirm 1970s 2D magnetism theory

featured_image.name: Exotic magnetic vortices observed in atom-thin crystal for ...

items.description: Physicists at the University of Texas at Austin have experimentally demonstrated the full sequence of exotic magnetic phases predicted by a theoretical model of two-dimensional magnetism first proposed in the 1970s, marking the first time the complete framework has been realized in a real material. The results were published in the journal Nature Materials.[1]

items.title: Trump won't rule out ground troops in Iran as strikes enter third day

featured_image.name: Donald Trump won't rule out boots on ground in Iran

items.description:
President Donald Trump on Monday declined to rule out deploying American ground forces to Iran, telling the New York Post he would send them "if necessary" as U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran continued into their third day under Operation Epic Fury.[1]

"I don't have the yips with respect to boots on the ground — like every president says, 'There will be no boots on the ground.' I don't say it," Trump told the Post. "I say 'probably don't need them,' [or] 'if they were necessary.'"[2][1]

At the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a similar tone during the first detailed briefing since the operation began on Saturday, refusing to specify what the administration would or would not do. "President Trump ensures that our enemies understand we'll go as far as we need to go to advance American interests," Hegseth said, appearing alongside Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine.[3][4]

items.title: Six US troops killed as Trump won't rule out ground forces in Iran

featured_image.name: War in the Mideast widens as Trump says strikes on Iran ...

items.description:
The United States is "not currently postured" to send ground forces into Iran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Monday, even as President Donald Trump refused to take the option off the table and the American military campaign entered its third day with mounting casualties on both sides.[1][2]

Rubio, speaking on Capitol Hill before briefing the congressional "Gang of Eight," said the administration is confident its objectives can be achieved through air and naval power alone. But in comments to the New York Post, Trump struck a different tone: "Probably don't need them," he said of ground troops, adding, "if they were necessary" — a stark departure from the traditional presidential assurance of "no boots on the ground."[3][4]

items.title: Iranian drones strike US Embassy in Riyadh, sparking fire

featured_image.name: Fire at US embassy complex in Riyadh after blast heard ...

items.description: A fire erupted at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh early Tuesday after two suspected Iranian drones struck the compound, according to a U.S. State Department cable reviewed by The Wall Street Journal. There were no immediate reports of injuries, and embassy personnel sheltered in place.[1][2]

items.title: Saudi Arabia goes on full military alert after Iranian drone strikes

featured_image.name: Return to Your Senses': Gulf States Ramp Up Iran Criticism ...

items.description:
Saudi Arabia raised its military readiness to "full alert" on Monday after Iranian drones struck the massive Ras Tanura refinery on the kingdom's Gulf coast, as the Gulf Cooperation Council condemned Tehran's attacks across six member states and warned it reserves the right to retaliate.[1][2]

The escalation came three days into a widening Middle East conflict that began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran. Tehran responded with volleys of missiles and drones targeting GCC nations that host American military installations, killing at least six people and injuring more than 100 across the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman, and Saudi Arabia.[3][2]

items.title: Ukraine says it recaptured more land than Russia seized in February

featured_image.name: Ukraine's military makes gains in southeast region of ...

items.description:
Ukrainian Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi announced on March 2 that Ukrainian defense forces reclaimed more territory in February than Russian troops managed to seize — the first time Kyiv has outpaced Moscow in territorial gains since the Kursk Oblast incursion into Russian territory in the summer of 2024.[1][2]

"In February 2026, for the first time since the Kursk offensive operation, the Ukrainian defence forces regained control of more territory than the enemy managed to capture," Syrskyi wrote on Telegram. "We have survived this difficult battle for winter."[2][1]

items.title: Rubio says Israel's strike plan triggered US attack on Iran

featured_image.name: US says Rubio to visit Israel on Monday to discuss Iran ...

items.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio disclosed Monday that the United States launched its attack on Iran after learning that Israel was determined to strike with or without American participation, a revelation that cast the joint military operation in a new light and raised fresh questions about the administration's legal justification for war.

"We knew that there was going to be an Israeli action. We knew that that would precipitate an attack against American forces, and we knew that if we didn't preemptively go after them before they launched those attacks, we would suffer higher casualties," Rubio told reporters on Capitol Hill before briefing congressional leaders.[1][2]

items.title: Trump refuses to rule out ground troops in Iran

featured_image.name: What is Trump's approval rating? Iran strikes controversial in polls

items.description:
President Donald Trump said Monday he would not rule out sending American ground troops into Iran, declaring that Operation Epic Fury is progressing faster than expected as the U.S. military campaign entered its third day with mounting casualties on both sides.

"I don't have the yips with respect to boots on the ground — like every president says, 'There will be no boots on the ground.' I don't say it," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published March 2. "I say 'probably don't need them,' or 'if they were necessary.'"[1][2]
